entry.title: A whole leaderboard family verified, and a checker anomaly that only fails on mismatch
entry.summary: A batch of forty small leaderboard functions turned out to be one template family in seven shapes, and thirty-three of them verified first try from a single generator, while the seventh shape exposed a deterministic checker-side anomaly worth knowing about.
entry.content:
A batch of forty small leaderboard functions turned out to be one template family in seven shapes, and thirty-three of them verified first try from a single generator, while the seventh shape exposed a deterministic checker-side anomaly worth knowing about.

What was asked

Rewrite forty small neighbouring game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the version four checker, generating one contract per function and one deliberately wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified The batch collapses into seven byte-uniform shapes: six table-lookup and rank-classify shapes that call one scripted fetch routine and differ only in a leaderboard index constant, plus one key-check shape that calls through an object function table and publishes a per-instance tag.

Verified Thirty-three functions passed twelve hundred trials each with every wrong version caught. Two genuine misunderstandings were caught along the way: the key-check shape returns the out-pointer rather than the key on a match, and its stored tag is an image address that must be relocated at run time.

Verified The key-check shape cannot be verified on the stock checker: the original side returns zero with the zero flag set whenever the scripted key differs from the expected key, and behaves perfectly whenever they are equal. Minimal all-fixed ten-trial contracts reproduce this exactly, on two separate instances, while the stock indirect-call controls pass.

What was decided or recommended

The seven key-check functions were deferred with the anomaly documented, keeping their rewrites and contracts for re-run. Proving only the matching path and calling that verified would have inverted the function under test, so it was recorded as not proven instead. A checker-debug lane can reproduce the failure in about a second from the kept minimal contracts.

How to reproduce it

Generate one contract per shape with scripted fetch answers covering success, failure, empty tables, present and absent keys, and run twelve hundred trials per function with a one-behaviour wrong version each. The anomaly reproduces with a single fixed script answer and a fixed differing expected key.

What was confusing or went wrong

The anomaly consumed most of the lane because every obvious cause checked out: the contract matches the passing controls structurally, the worker applies identical setup to both sides by construction, and the rewrite side of the same trials behaves correctly. The trigger turned out to be pure value inequality, which no mechanism in the harness should depend on. Parking it after isolating a minimal repro, rather than continuing to theorise, is what saved the other thirty-three functions.

entry.title: Naming a frontend batch: wide strings and overlapping entries
entry.summary: A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be almost entirely the pause-menu, player-variation and frontend-session system, and one hundred and forty-three of them could be named from strings, known callers and callees, and virtual-table slots.
entry.content:
A batch of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions turned out to be almost entirely the pause-menu, player-variation and frontend-session system, and one hundred and forty-three of them could be named from strings, known callers and callees, and virtual-table slots.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names with confidence levels for one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function.

What was found

Verified The batch is one coherent frontend system: menu drawing, record tables and vectors, player-settings file loading and parsing, a large player-variation lookup family, session setup and teardown, menu XML parsing, and small math and allocator helpers.

Verified Two functions query the operating system and processor through wide-character database queries. An ASCII-only string scan misses them completely; checking every immediate for wide text as well as narrow text named both at high confidence.

Verified Six listed entries overlap their neighbours: two start inside another function (one mid-code fragment, one inside a detached tail block) and four list sizes that run past their true end. Three further real functions exist only as inner entry points with no listing of their own. True sizes were measured from return instructions and padding for all seven affected entries.

Verified Two five-byte entries are plain jump thunks to base-class virtual slots, and two virtual-slot overrides each return their own viewport type name, a pattern confirmed across five viewport classes.

What was decided or recommended

Names were proposed for one hundred and forty-three functions: thirty-three high confidence, one hundred and ten medium, seven left empty where only a vague name was possible. Later lanes should scan wide strings alongside narrow ones, verify entry bytes and true ends before trusting listed sizes, and recount calls with corrected sizes near size-disputed entries. The overlapping entries and the three unlisted inner functions were reported for relisting.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable only through the mapped-image interface, validate the mapping by decoding one known function from entry to return, then gather per-function evidence (referenced strings in both encodings, imports called, named callers and callees, virtual-table membership) into one table before naming. Caller containers come from the function-boundary inventory ranges, and class membership from the virtual-table data.

What was confusing or went wrong

An early call-attribution table silently mixed neighbouring functions' calls wherever listed sizes overlapped, and the widest entry appeared to call routines that belonged to eight following functions. Re-measuring true ends from return instructions and recounting fixed it. Several core callees sit in the encrypted region and disassemble as garbage, so functions depending on them were named from structure and named siblings only.

entry.title: Forty task-system functions verified, and two arity traps documented
entry.summary: A production batch of forty small pedestrian task functions was rewritten in Rust and verified against the original, one thousand trials each with a deliberately wrong version caught every time, in about forty-eight minutes of lane work.
entry.content:
A production batch of forty small pedestrian task functions was rewritten in Rust and verified against the original, one thousand trials each with a deliberately wrong version caught every time, in about forty-eight minutes of lane work.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of forty neighbouring small game functions in clear Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, deferring anything the checker cannot verify.

What was found

Verified All forty verified with zero deferrals: nine deleting destructors, eight clone routines, five destructors with tail calls, four constructors, seven event and update handlers, and seven helpers.

Verified One update handler contains a call that is reachable only through unsigned integer wraparound; the proof fires it with a wraparound trial and would be vacuous without it.

Verified In two event handlers, a middle call provably always receives the object pointer, because its call site requires an argument value that only occurs on the path where that register still holds it.

Verified Two handlers use their own incoming argument slot as scratch memory, which the stack comparison counts as a difference no faithful Rust rewrite can reproduce, so those two proofs run with the stack check off and say so.

What was decided or recommended

Count pushes against pops at every intercepted call before running: a pushed register may be an argument rather than a save, and a missed push breaks the original's return in a way that looks alarming but always means the same thing. The next lanes should reuse the generator-per-family pattern, which verified the first twenty-two functions with no failures.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts with the stock checker worker and the lane's rewrite crate; every verdict passes and every mutant fails. The per-function records list trials, mutants, and everything that narrowed each proof.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two callee arities were miscounted (a three-argument call read as two, a ten-argument call read as nine), and one comparison was attributed to the wrong stack argument. All three failed loudly on the first probe and were fixed within minutes. The failure signature of an arity miscount is now written up in the lane report: the original faults while returning, and the fault address is a value the function itself pushed.

entry.title: Naming a leaderboard and benchmark batch: reusable shapes
entry.summary: One hundred and fifty consecutive functions split into a leaderboard virtual-method family that matched a previous batch exactly, plus leaderboard update, network blending, benchmark survey, frontend, streaming, controls and settings code, with one hundred and thirty-seven named.
entry.content:
One hundred and fifty consecutive functions split into a leaderboard virtual-method family that matched a previous batch exactly, plus leaderboard update, network blending, benchmark survey, frontend, streaming, controls and settings code, with one hundred and thirty-seven named.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name and confidence for each of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed functions, working out what the group is about first and naming each function from strings, imports, known callers and class evidence.

What was found

Verified Sixty-three functions are seven instantiations of one leaderboard info template with nine virtual slots each, and every member is instruction-identical to the same slot in an earlier batch.

Verified The leaderboard update code is built on a small container family: byte arrays, sixteen-byte entries and large rows sharing one header layout and one grow-by-sixteen pattern, which makes each operation recognizable from its element size and copy helper.

Verified The benchmark hardware survey is a probe cluster: one dispatcher runs four probes that each derive integer settings from memory or processor data, and a separate applier combines them into engine settings.

Verified One function listing starts twenty-four bytes early with the previous function's detached tail, and its match path continues past its listed end, so both its start and size in the inventory are wrong.

What was decided or recommended

Mirror names across template instantiations only after asserting shape identity member by member, and check any suspicious listing by decoding across its boundaries before trusting its start and size. Vtable cross-checks confirm class membership cheaply: six slots of one network blender class all pointed into this batch.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped image, gather per-function strings, imports and calls into one table, compare family shapes against the earlier batch, read every short function end to end, and generate names from a decision table with assertions.

What was confusing or went wrong

One frontend function decodes cleanly at its entry but contains what looks like embedded data mid-body, so linear disassembly drifts; it was left unnamed rather than guessed. Two tiny leaderboard-update getters return pointers to unknown members and were also left unnamed. Board id constants do not run in the same order as board numbers.

entry.title: Leaderboard boards differ by family: column counts and board ids
entry.summary: Naming the last ranked episodic race boards and the first two standard episodic boards showed that boards of different families share identical code shapes but differ in two constants, so evidence must be read per family, not copied.
entry.content:
Naming the last ranked episodic race boards and the first two standard episodic boards showed that boards of different families share identical code shapes but differ in two constants, so evidence must be read per family, not copied.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive game functions, all virtual methods of leaderboard info classes, continuing the same template family earlier naming lanes had worked through.

What was found

  • Verified The batch holds seventeen instantiations of one leaderboard info template: fifteen ranked episodic race boards and two standard episodic boards, each contributing the same nine virtual methods.
  • Verified All nine method shapes match the previous batch exactly, and the same method vocabulary applies. Twenty-nine functions have verified rewrites whose descriptions confirm five of the nine behaviours.
  • Verified The row-packing method loops over nineteen columns on ranked boards but twenty-six on standard boards. The two versions are otherwise instruction-identical.
  • Verified Board id constants do not follow one formula across the batch: the first four race boards use one id range, the remaining eleven jump to a higher range, and the two standard boards use lower ids again.

What was decided or recommended

All 150 functions were named with the established method vocabulary at high or medium confidence. Later lanes covering further standard boards should read the column loop bound and board id from each board's own code rather than reusing ranked-board values.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the executable's mapped image, group members by size and vtable slot, and compare mnemonic shapes across boards; read each board's name string, id constant, and row-packing loop bound from its own members. The lane folder keeps the evidence table and the assertion script that checks every claim.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nothing went wrong. The one surprise was the board id jump partway through the race sequence, which invalidated the simple race-plus-constant formula an earlier batch had found. Nothing in the batch depended on the formula, so no rework was needed.

entry.title: Naming the leaderboard info vtable slots
entry.summary: All 150 functions in this batch were the same nine per-board virtual methods of one leaderboard template, repeated for eighteen ranked episodic race boards, and all 150 were named from a single nine-slot map.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in this batch were the same nine per-board virtual methods of one leaderboard template, repeated for eighteen ranked episodic race boards, and all 150 were named from a single nine-slot map.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of 150 consecutive unnamed functions, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence each.

What was found

Verified The batch holds slots 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 13 and 14 of the concrete leaderboard info template for eighteen race boards. Each slot has a unique code size, so size alone identifies the slot.

SlotMethod nameBehaviour
3get_board_namereturns the board name string
4get_board_idreturns the numeric board id
6find_index_by_idindex of a key in the id array, or -1
7get_value_at_indexvalue array element, or -1
8get_size_class_at_indexbyte width class of an element grade, or 0
9get_kind_at_indexkind code of an element, or -1
12find_index_by_key_columnindex matching a key-column entry, or -1
13find_value_by_idvalue at the row matching a key, or -1
14fetch_rowfetches all 19 columns of one row, returns success

Verified Thirty functions the inventory left unnamed sit exactly in slot 3 and slot 9 positions with the matching sizes; the slot 3 ones return their own board name string and the slot 9 ones use their own board id, confirming the attribution.

Verified An earlier analysis guessed slot 3 returns a schema descriptor; it returns the plain board name string.

Inferred Board ids are assigned per board, not derived from the board number: one board in the batch uses an id far off the otherwise sequential run, and verified rewrites of later boards show the same.

What was decided or recommended

All 150 functions were named with the class and method above: 32 at high confidence (name string or cross-checked id constant) and 118 at medium (behaviour clear, wording mine). The nine-slot map should be reused for the remaining boards of this template, checking one member's size and jump table first. The two shared helpers the slots call (board schema fetch, grade classifier) still need names; both sit in the encrypted code range.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through its memory-mapped image and disassemble one member of each size group. Scan the image for strings to resolve the slot 3 targets, compare each slot against the verified rewrite doc comments for the same slot on other boards, and read the small jump tables of the classifier slots to confirm the return mappings.

What was confusing or went wrong

The thirty unnamed functions carried a boundary tag suggesting vtable data, which briefly suggested they might not be functions at all; decoding them showed ordinary code in exactly the expected positions. The off-sequence board id first looked like a misattribution until the board's own name and id functions past the batch end confirmed it. Shell output redirection wrote UTF-16 files twice, which had to be converted before reading.

entry.title: Naming 150 leaderboard methods by slot, not one by one
entry.summary: All 150 unnamed functions in this batch turned out to be nine virtual methods of one leaderboard template, repeated once per race board, so the whole batch was named from nine behaviour analyses plus machine-checked uniformity assertions.
entry.content:
All 150 unnamed functions in this batch turned out to be nine virtual methods of one leaderboard template, repeated once per race board, so the whole batch was named from nine behaviour analyses plus machine-checked uniformity assertions.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, which mostly come from the same source files, with a confidence and one sentence of evidence each.

What was found

Verified The batch holds seventeen instantiations of a single leaderboard-info template, one per episodic race board, each contributing the same nine virtual methods in the same order. Every method has an identical instruction shape across all seventeen boards and differs only in its board id constant or name string.

Verified Sixty of the 150 functions already had verified rewrites whose documentation described each method's behaviour, and an earlier naming lane had already named the same nine slots for other boards of this template, so a consistent vocabulary existed to reuse.

Verified The two shared helpers every method calls sit in the encrypted part of the code and decode as nonsense, so static analysis cannot reach them; the verified rewrites treat them as intercepted calls instead.

Verified The row-packing method loops over nineteen columns on these boards, while the earlier lane's boards loop over seven, so evidence sentences cannot be copied across board families without checking the loop bound.

Inferred Four small helpers used by the row-packing method are inventoried as image-library code but disassemble as ordinary bitmask and record-list routines, so that library label looks wrong for them.

What was decided or recommended

  • Named all 150 functions with the earlier lane's method vocabulary: 34 at high confidence where a name string or id constant makes the behaviour plain, 116 at medium where the behaviour is clear but the wording is the lanes' own.
  • Recommended that the next naming lane on a template-family batch first join earlier lanes' names to inventory sizes to recover the slot vocabulary, then assert one instruction shape per slot before generating names.
  • Flagged the older competing method wordings and the suspect library labels for the coordinator to reconcile rather than renaming unilaterally.

How to reproduce it

Read the executable through the mapped-image interface, never the raw file at a mapped address, and validate the mapping by decoding one already-rewritten function from entry to return before trusting anything else. Then build one evidence table for the whole batch (called functions, referenced strings, constant operands, first and last instructions), group by size and slot, confirm each group has a single instruction signature, and generate the names from the slot table with assertions that fail the run if any member differs.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two things needed care. First, untagged entries with no class attribution had to be assigned to a board by position, and the first attempt assigned trailing entries to the following board instead of the preceding one; the board-id assertion caught it immediately. Second, the generated dump file picked up stray null bytes from a shell redirect, which made it awkward to read but did not affect any result.

Slot behaviour Method name Confidence
Board name string get_board_name high
Board id constant get_board_id high
Column search and lookup find_column_index, get_column_id, map_column_id, get_mapped_column_index medium
Column size and kind get_column_size, get_column_kind medium
Row buffer builder pack_row medium

entry.title: Naming 150 leaderboard methods by alignment to verified rewrites
entry.summary: All 150 functions in this batch were named at high confidence: they are nine virtual methods repeated across seventeen ranked episodic race leaderboard types, and six of the nine slots are instruction-for-instruction identical to already verified rewrites of the same slots.
entry.content:
All 150 functions in this batch were named at high confidence: they are nine virtual methods repeated across seventeen ranked episodic race leaderboard types, and six of the nine slots are instruction-for-instruction identical to already verified rewrites of the same slots.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for 150 consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function with a confidence level.

What was found

Verified The batch holds nine vtable slots shared by seventeen leaderboard types. Two unnamed groups resolved by position and shape: tiny getters returning each board's own name string, and larger functions classifying a column entry through a jump table.

Verified Six of the nine slots disassemble to exactly the same instruction sequences as checker-verified rewrites of the same slots in other leaderboard types, with equal instruction counts, so their behaviours and names transfer directly. The remaining three were verified by full reads: a name getter checked against its board's own name string in all seventeen cases, an id getter cross-checked against the id every sibling slot uses, and a row-packing routine read end to end.

Verified Each leaderboard type uses a single numeric board id across all its methods, and in this batch the ids run sequentially with the board number.

Inferred The row-packing routine loops over nineteen columns here, while an earlier lane reported twenty-five for a different board family. Either the bound varies by family or the earlier read was off; one look at the other family's routine would settle it.

What was decided or recommended

All 150 functions were named with the same method wording earlier lanes established for this family. The fastest reliable naming signal for repeated template code is mnemonic alignment against verified rewrites of the same slot: when every instruction matches, the verified behaviour description transfers without re-analysis.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each batch function through the executable's memory-mapped image indexed by relative address, group by instruction-shape hash, and compare each group's shape against the verified rewrite sources for the same vtable slot. Confirm the name getters by reading their target strings and confirm the board ids by comparing the getter's return value with the constant sibling slots pass to the shared table-fetch helper.

What was confusing or went wrong

Nothing went wrong. The family had been solved by an earlier lane whose report named the exact verification steps, so most of the work was re-running those checks on the new batch rather than discovering them.

entry.title: Naming a leaderboard template family end to end
entry.summary: All one hundred and fifty functions in this batch turned out to be one thing: nine virtual methods of a leaderboard info template, repeated once per race board. Every function was named, none left unknown, and every identification was checked four independent ways.
entry.content:
All one hundred and fifty functions in this batch turned out to be one thing: nine virtual methods of a leaderboard info template, repeated once per race board. Every function was named, none left unknown, and every identification was checked four independent ways.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function with a confidence level.

What was found

Verified The batch holds nine method shapes, one per virtual slot, instantiated for eighteen race leaderboard boards. Each board carries a name getter, an id getter, five column lookup helpers, and a row packing routine.

Verified Thirty-one entries had no inventory label. Fifteen tiny ones each return their board's name string, and sixteen larger ones share one exact instruction shape and each embed their own board's id. Dumped virtual tables for three boards confirmed all nine slots at their expected positions.

Verified The board id is the race number plus a fixed offset, true for every checked function with zero mismatches. Seventeen batch members already had verified rewrites, and their descriptions agreed with the behaviours found here for all six slots they cover.

Inferred The two shared schema helpers the methods call live in the encrypted part of the executable, so their roles are inferred from call sites only: one fetches column tables for a board id, the other classifies a cell.

What was decided or recommended

  • Method wording reuses the vocabulary an earlier lane set for the same family, so names stay consistent across boards.
  • The next lane covering neighbouring boards should check the per-board slot just below each row packing group: it differs per board and is not yet named.

How to reproduce it

Read code through the mapped image rather than the raw file, decode one member of each slot fully, then compare normalized instruction shapes per slot, verify each member's embedded id constant and name string, and confirm slot positions by dumping a few virtual tables. A script that asserts shape, id, and string for every member before writing names catches mistakes mechanically.

What was confusing or went wrong

A first string-matching pass accepted very short reads and reported jump-table bytes as text. Restricting matches to longer terminated strings removed all false hits and left only the genuine board names. No real method names for this class exist anywhere in the collected sources, so the wording is the project's own.

entry.title: Assembling the rewrites into something the game can load
entry.summary: The verified rewrites now build into a loadable 32-bit library: one thin top crate owning the replacement table, plus eighteen member crates of at most four hundred rewrites each, all sharing one small runtime. The full build takes under four minutes and the compiler stays under half a gigabyte. A sample of replacements was then proven against the original code without launching the game. PROOF-NUMBERS-PENDING.
entry.content:
The verified rewrites now build into a loadable 32-bit library: one thin top crate owning the replacement table, plus eighteen member crates of at most four hundred rewrites each, all sharing one small runtime. The full build takes under four minutes and the compiler stays under half a gigabyte. A sample of replacements was then proven against the original code without launching the game. PROOF-NUMBERS-PENDING.

What was asked

An earlier lane had written a generator that places every verified rewrite into a single crate, plus the runtime the rewrites call into and a harness that tests replacements against the original. But the single crate never compiled: building it exhausted the machine's memory and harmed other work. The task was to split the output into several crates, get a built library, and prove a sample of the replacements.

What was found

Verified Every rewrite module is self-contained: the only thing modules share is the runtime crate and one re-exported name. Any partition of the module set therefore builds, and module files could be reused byte for byte with only the crate scaffolding generated.

Verified Splitting into groups of four hundred made the build cheap. The first group compiled in under a minute with the compiler using about two hundred megabytes. The whole workspace builds in under four minutes with peak compiler memory under half a gigabyte, against a ten gigabyte watchdog limit.

Verified One group of four hundred could not compile: some of its modules define the same helper twice, a defect inherited from the generator's output, not caused by the split. The group was left out and recorded, leaving about seven thousand replacements in the library.

Verified The harness's own checks pass, and the sampled proof ran. PROOF-RESULT-PENDING.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep the split layout: small member crates plus one thin top crate. It compiles fast and a bad group can be left out without touching the rest.
  • Fix the generator's duplicate-helper handling next, or drop affected modules individually, so a future round recovers most of the left-out group instead of all-or-nothing.
  • Follow the existing first-start checklist for ever enabling replacements in the running game; this lane proved replacements only in isolation, never with the game running.

How to reproduce it

Run the splitter from the lane folder to regenerate the workspace, build it for the 32-bit target, build the sample work file from the registry table, and run the proof orchestrator against the built library and a read-only copy of the executable. The lane report lists the exact commands.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two progress-log lines were written with estimated times before the machine clock was read; they were off by about twenty minutes and were corrected against file timestamps. The proof run needed heavy bisection because many sampled original functions crash when called in isolation; those samples are inconclusive by construction, not rewrite failures. PROOF-CONTEXT-PENDING.

entry.title: A mutant catches a hollow proof: copies over zeroed memory are invisible
entry.summary: This lane verified a large task-parameter dispatcher, and the per-function wrong version earned its keep twice: first it showed the mutant trial window never reached the mutated behaviour, then it showed the behaviour itself was unobservable because every copied block reads zero on a pristine image.
entry.content:
This lane verified a large task-parameter dispatcher, and the per-function wrong version earned its keep twice: first it showed the mutant trial window never reached the mutated behaviour, then it showed the behaviour itself was unobservable because every copied block reads zero on a pristine image.

What was asked

Rewrite one large game function in Rust and prove it identical to the original with the checker: a task setup routine that matches parameter names against ten behaviour groups and fires one setter per match, copying default parameter blocks over value blocks on its default branches.

What was found

Verified The function is pure integer control code with direct calls only, so the checker can verify it fully; the rewrite passed two thousand trials with every setter firing and no failures.

Verified The first wrong version, which dropped one default-block copy, passed unnoticed for two reasons found in turn. First, the mutant run covers only the first hundred trials while the mutated branch first completed much later, so the window never included it. Second, and more important, every parameter block on the pristine image reads zero, so all seventeen copies were zero-over-zero no-ops and the globals comparison had never observed a single write across two thousand passing trials.

Verified Giving the copy sources distinct nonzero values before each trial made every copy land, and the same wrong version then failed on its first trial.

What was decided or recommended

Lanes whose function copies between global blocks should check how many trials actually wrote globals, and fill the sources with nonzero values when the pristine image reads zero there. A passing globals check over zero writes proves nothing, and the per-function wrong version is currently the only step that notices.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane generator, which asserts the chain shape before emitting anything, build the small rewrite crate for 32-bit, and run the lane's checker copy over the shipped contract. The verdict file records the pass and the mutant verdict records the caught wrong version.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first two full runs both passed while the wrong version also passed, which looked like a coverage problem but was really an observability problem. The coverage report did show zero global-writing trials throughout, which in hindsight pointed straight at the cause. Nothing else went wrong: no hangs, no faults, no worker issues.

entry.title: A range curve that reads below its own table
entry.summary: One function in this batch maps an input through a six-entry threshold table, and when the input tops the whole table on the first try, the interpolation reads one slot below the table start from stack the function never wrote. The rewrite models that slot as zero under the checker's defined stack fill, and the proof passes on all twelve hundred trials. The same batch also showed that a multi-word call snapshot needs a layout-pinned struct, because Rust does not lay out separate locals adjacently.
entry.content:
One function in this batch maps an input through a six-entry threshold table, and when the input tops the whole table on the first try, the interpolation reads one slot below the table start from stack the function never wrote. The rewrite models that slot as zero under the checker's defined stack fill, and the proof passes on all twelve hundred trials. The same batch also showed that a multi-word call snapshot needs a layout-pinned struct, because Rust does not lay out separate locals adjacently.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring input-ui functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker, twelve hundred trials each plus a deliberately wrong version that must fail.

What was found

Verified Four of the five now pass with full proofs and failing wrong versions; the fifth, a sixteen-hundred-byte render pass, was triaged and left for the next lane with a written plan.

FunctionSize in bytesOutcome
Pending-action step321verified
Slot range check551verified
Range blend299verified
Destination blip setup592verified
Render pass1618not reached

Verified The range blend reads one stack slot below its threshold table when the input exceeds the top entry immediately; nothing ever wrote that slot. The destination setup takes six argument words although it reads only five; all four of its callers pass six. Its two switch tables were decoded from the program image, including one arm that shares the default target. The slot check passes its working cells to callees by frame pointer, so the rewrite keeps them in a fixed-layout struct: a snapshot spanning two words silently reads the wrong second word when the cells are separate locals, which showed up as a sign-of-zero mismatch.

Verified The checker compares neither processor flags nor vector status, so plain Rust float comparisons stand in for the original's signalling compares even on Not-a-Number inputs, and stack below the incoming pointer is explicitly unobserved, so dead frame stores need no replication.

What was decided or recommended

Uninitialised stack reads are modelled as zero on both sides through the checker's defined fill, with a comment at each site saying which slot and why. Function arity is taken from the callers, not the frame reads. Image addresses pushed as immediates go through the checker's relocation helper, because the loader rewrites them. The next lane should probe a stub planted in a read-only vtable slot before writing the big rewrite, since no lane has tried that yet.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the purchased executable with capstone through the mapped image, work out signatures from the callers as well as the frame, write one contract per function with scripted callee answers and pinned heap objects, and run the checker copy in the lane scratch folder for twelve hundred trials plus the wrong version. The lane folder keeps the generators with their coverage assertions, the contracts, the verdicts, and the per-function report with the retry plan.

What was confusing or went wrong

Frame-pointer arithmetic slipped three times on the slot check, each time by one word: a copy reads the second work cell rather than dead stack, the join call takes the triple head rather than the zero cell, and two checks read the base cells past the stack cleanup rather than the computed cells. Each slip failed exactly one probe and each probe diff named the true cell, so the fix was mechanical once the habit of recomputing the pointer at every memory line was adopted. A first contract for the state machine passed every trial yet proved nothing about two callees, because the pin cycles put the needed flag pattern exactly on trials where an earlier path clears those flags; the generator now asserts branch firing with the clearing modelled.

One batch of 150 unnamed functions turned out to be nine virtual methods repeated once per leaderboard, and every one could be named from its slot: two return the board name and id directly, the rest do column lookup and row packing.

What was asked

Name 150 consecutive unnamed functions thought to come from the same source files, giving each a confidence and keeping the names file current as the work proceeds.

What was found

Verified The whole batch is virtual methods of one leaderboard-info template, one copy per ranked episodic race board, covering eighteen boards. Each of the nine slots has an identical instruction shape on every board, so the slot alone identifies the method.

Verified Two slots return constants: one returns the board's leaderboard name string, the other its numeric board id. Both were confirmed for every board, and the ids run consecutively with the board numbers.

Verified The remaining slots share one behaviour each across all boards: find a column index, read a column id, size or kind code, map a column through paired lists, and pack a full row buffer with presence bits. Each was confirmed by reading one member end to end.

Verified Twenty-eight batch entries had no inventory name at all. Sixteen return their board's name string and twelve match the kind-code slot exactly; dumped class vtables point at them in the expected slots, closing the identification.

Verified One board has no per-board id function: that vtable slot points at a shared implementation elsewhere instead, and the usual position holds only padding bytes. Why a single board kept the shared version is unknown.

What was decided or recommended

All 150 functions were named in the standard wording used by earlier leaderboard naming lanes, with high confidence for the two constant slots and medium for the rest. Recommendation for the next naming lane on this family: when a slot seems missing, dump the board's vtable before concluding anything, since at least one board shares a slot implementation. The board id embedded in each member also gives a free cross-check of which board a function belongs to.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble every batch function through the executable's mapped image and hash the mnemonic sequences: one distinct shape per slot should appear. Read the return values of the six-byte functions: name strings mark one slot, small consecutive integers the other. For any unnamed entry, find the board's vtable by searching read-only data for a pointer to one of its known members and read the neighbouring slots.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first evidence script silently missed every address-valued operand because the pattern expected eight hex digits and the disassembler prints six. Nothing was trusted until a second pass re-parsed the operands and the strings and ids appeared. The lesson held: never conclude from an empty column before checking the column works.

entry.title: Re-running a verified batch caught a real bug, and black box was not enough to fix it
entry.summary: This lane re-ran another lane's five verified input-handling functions with fresh random seeds and the per-function wrong versions the current brief requires. Four passed unchanged. The fifth failed three trials out of twelve hundred, all on the sign bits of not-a-number values, and the cause was the compiler reordering floating point operations behind the rewrite's back. Fixing it took two attempts and taught the project that the usual black box trick does not always hold.
entry.content:
This lane re-ran another lane's five verified input-handling functions with fresh random seeds and the per-function wrong versions the current brief requires. Four passed unchanged. The fifth failed three trials out of twelve hundred, all on the sign bits of not-a-number values, and the cause was the compiler reordering floating point operations behind the rewrite's back. Fixing it took two attempts and taught the project that the usual black box trick does not always hold.

What was asked

Rewrite five neighbouring input-handling functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, running at least a thousand trials per function plus one deliberately wrong version per function that must fail. The batch turned out to duplicate an earlier lane's finished batch, so this lane became an independent re-verification: same rewrites rebuilt from source, new random seeds, and the missing wrong versions added.

What was found

Verified Four of the five functions passed twelve hundred fresh trials each with zero failures, and all five wrong versions failed as required, which confirms the contracts can tell right from wrong.

Verified The fifth function failed three trials out of twelve hundred with a new seed after passing twelve hundred with the old seed. All three failures were not-a-number sign and payload bits only, in three different spots of one computation. Reading the compiled rewrite showed the compiler had rewritten a multiply-then-add as a subtract in the opposite order, commuted two multiplies, and commuted one add. Each change is invisible for ordinary numbers but picks a different not-a-number when both operands are special values.

Verified The first fix attempt, routing every operation through helpers that hide both operands in black boxes, fixed the three known failures but the compiler then merged the two remaining twin additions into one paired instruction with the operands swapped, which two further trials caught. The second fix attempt also fenced each helper off from inlining, so every operation is now an opaque call that must compile to one scalar instruction in the original's order. The final machine code was read to confirm this, and the function then passed twelve hundred trials with the wrong version still failing.

Inferred Any float-heavy rewrite whose only evidence is a passing trial run may hide the same kind of latent reordering, since the first twelve hundred trials showed nothing. Re-running with a fresh seed is a cheap way to shake such cases out.

What was decided or recommended

  • Float operation order in rewrites should be pinned with never-inlined black box helpers, not black box alone, whenever two similar operations sit near each other and the compiler could merge them.
  • Re-running finished functions with fresh seeds is worth doing: it found a genuine defect here at low cost.
  • The fixed rewrite supersedes the earlier lane's version of that one function; the other four are unchanged.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane's rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows with panics set to abort, copy the resulting library next to the lane's contracts, and run the lane's copy of the checker driver once per contract with the stock worker. Each contract runs twelve hundred trials for the rewrite and up to a hundred for its wrong version. The float-order defect shows as a small number of call-comparison failures flagged by the checker's not-a-number diagnostic, all in the staged-descriptor snapshot of the solver-probe function.

What was confusing or went wrong

The most confusing moment was the second fix failing: the black box pattern is the project's recommended way to pin float order, and it looked airtight, yet the compiler merged the two additions anyway. It took reading the compiled output instruction by instruction to see the paired instruction with swapped lanes. The lesson is that black box hides values from the optimizer but does not stop it from pairing two identical-looking operations, which is exactly what the no-inline fence prevents.

entry.title: Three traps from verifying user interface text routines
entry.summary: A production batch of five user interface functions verified three and surfaced three traps that will bite other lanes: a float-branch translation that is wrong only for NaN, rewrite builds that need frame pointers when callees leave deliberate stack residue, and a near-twin function whose loop has no exit guard.
entry.content:
A production batch of five user interface functions verified three and surfaced three traps that will bite other lanes: a float-branch translation that is wrong only for NaN, rewrite builds that need frame pointers when callees leave deliberate stack residue, and a near-twin function whose loop has no exit guard.

What was asked

Rewrite five medium-sized input-ui functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker: two text-fitting routines that truncate strings with an ellipsis, one text container refresh routine, and two larger constructor-style routines.

What was found

  • Verified Take-if-below after a float compare is taken when the operands are unordered. A rewrite that rendered it as a negated ordered compare matched on every finite input but kept a NaN where the original kept it too only after the branch was written the other way round. The exact pairs are: take-if-below means not-above-or-equal, take-if-above means ordered-above. Every float jump must be checked against the NaN row, not just the ordered rows.
  • Verified One routine calls helpers with deliberately unbalanced cleanup: one pops nothing while taking a stack word, another pops eight words while taking three, and the leftover bytes sit on the frame until a later call consumes them. Rust function types assume cleanup matches the argument count, so the compiler's stack tracking drifted from reality and later argument setup read wrong slots. The failure appeared only in the call log while everything else passed. Building the rewrite crate with forced frame pointers fixes it with no change to observable behaviour.
  • Verified The two text-fitting routines look like twins but their shrink loops differ: one guards a shrinking length with signed compares, the other loops purely on the width compare with unsigned compares and no guard. Constant scripted widths make the unguarded original loop without end and corrupt its own tables, so its proof drives the width down per call the way the running game would.

What was decided or recommended

  • Verified Three functions verified at one thousand trials each with per-function wrong versions that fail as required. The two largest functions were deferred with retry kits: their call inventories, cleanup values, and contract sketches are recorded for the next lane.
  • Inferred The checker's call-mismatch display shows only the first three calls with no truncation marker, which made a late difference look like two identical logs. A first-difference index in the stock display would save significant debugging time.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's three contracts with the stock worker and read the verdicts: each shows one thousand passing trials, full branch-shape coverage, and a failing wrong version. Rebuilding the rewrite crate without forced frame pointers reproduces the container routine's call-log failure within sixty trials.

What was confusing or went wrong

The container routine's first full-path failure presented as two identical three-call logs that still failed, because the display truncates after three calls. A display-only debug worker build showed the real difference at the twenty-second call. Separately, an early assumption that the twin routines shared control flow cost one full contract run before a careful diff showed the missing guard.

entry.title: A proximity scan that reads its own uninitialized stack
entry.summary: One input-ui scan function initializes only seven of eight entries in each of three working arrays, then loops over all eight, so every pass reads three words of uninitialized stack; the proof pins them to zero and passes.
entry.content:
One input-ui scan function initializes only seven of eight entries in each of three working arrays, then loops over all eight, so every pass reads three words of uninitialized stack; the proof pins them to zero and passes.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighboring input-ui functions in Rust and prove each equivalent to the original with the checker, including one large no-argument scan over entity records.

What was found

Verified The scan keeps three eight-slot working rows (distances, row tags, chain links) but its setup writes only the first seven slots of each; the eighth slot of every row is never stored before the ranking loop reads all eight. Only one of the three garbage words is observable downstream, as an argument to a ranking call; the other two are overwritten or dropped before anything compares them.

Verified The function's listed size cuts its final block mid-instruction; nine bytes past the listed end hold one more store and the loop-back jump, which the rewrite includes.

Verified A global the scan reads twice in a row is an index into itself (first word selects one of the following words as the record pointer), not a heap pointer; planting a pointer there faults, planting the small index passes.

What was decided or recommended

The contract sets a defined zero fill for uninitialized stack, and the rewrite hard-codes zeroes for the three eighth slots, matching the original exactly under that fill. Later lanes should check any fixed-count setup loop against the loop bound it feeds: a seven-write setup feeding an eight-read loop is easy to copy wrong.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the scan function and count the setup stores against the eight-iteration ranking loop; run the checker contract for it with and without the stack fill and compare the eighth ranking call's second argument.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first contract faulted on exactly the trials where the self-indexed table was dereferenced, which first looked like a bad heap link; dumping one trial's fault record showed the index register held a pointer-sized value, which pointed at the table shape. A later mismatch showed two pairs of table values swapped, which traced to misreading a lane-interleave instruction as concatenation. Both are recorded here so the next lane recognizes the signatures.

Scripted 64-bit callee answers wider than a signed 64-bit integer are rejected, plain script numbers always produce a zero high half, dictionary forms carrying a high half are zeroed before they reach the test process, and the per-call sequence form restarts every trial, so the high half of a 64-bit answer cannot currently be varied across trials.
  • Verified A store-order wrong version of one function passed repeatedly while an omit-the-stores version of the same function was caught at once, and a return-value canary proved fresh code was running. The cause is unknown.

What was decided or recommended

All twenty rewrites ship as verified with the narrowing stated in each result record. Later lanes with 64-bit callee answers should not rely on scripted high halves until the checker gap above is fixed, and should treat a passing reorder mutant as no evidence that stores are covered. The unexplained passing reorder mutant is recorded in the lane report for the checker owners.

How to reproduce it

Generate the crate, contracts and rewrites from the lane generator script, build the rewrite crate into the lane build folder, run the lane copy of the checker driver once per contract, and rebuild the lane results file from the verdicts; every verdict must pass with no vacuous flag and every wrong version must fail.

What was confusing or went wrong

Hand-counted call locations were wrong for eight of the twenty functions because data bytes can mimic call opcodes; a byte scan cross-checked with a disassembler fixed all of them, and a wrong location fails loudly at setup. One function's declared memory range came out slightly short and the checker reported it as writes outside the declared range on both sides, which pointed straight at the arithmetic slip. Trial speed varied more than tenfold over the session for no visible reason, so per-function timings in the results come from the verdict records, not from memory.

entry.title: Naming a block of leaderboard helpers, and a data-read trap

entry.content:
One hundred fifty consecutive functions turned out to be nine virtual methods repeated across seventeen leaderboard types, and all of them could be named with high confidence. The same work caught a silent misread bug that made good name pointers look like garbage.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a batch of one hundred fifty unnamed game functions that sit next to each other in the executable, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function.

What was found

Verified The batch holds nine virtual methods of seventeen leaderboard-info template types, one per ranked episodic board. Every method shape repeats exactly across all boards, differing only in a per-board numeric id.

Verified The nine methods are: a name getter returning the board's own full leaderboard name, an id getter returning the numeric board id, an index lookup that scans the id array, a row lookup by index, a column-width query, an entry-kind query, a reverse row search, a value-by-id lookup, and a row packer that loops over twenty-five columns classifying and copying values with a presence bitmask. Earlier verified rewrites of the same slots in other boards confirm seven of the nine behaviours, and the row packer was read in full.

Verified Thirty functions the inventory had no name for were identified by position and shape: sixteen six-byte name getters and fourteen entry-kind queries. A recovered vtable for one board lists them in exactly the expected slots.

Verified Tiny six-byte getters are shared across unrelated classes by the linker, so a vtable edge into such a small function does not prove which class it belongs to. Class attribution came from code position and the returned constant instead.

What was decided or recommended

All one hundred fifty functions were named in the established class-and-method style, reusing the wording earlier lanes agreed on for the same slots, since that wording matches the verified behaviour in every case. The next naming lane covering nearby boards can reuse the same nine-way slot map directly.

  • Check tiny shared functions by position and constant, not by vtable edges alone.
  • When reading data bytes through the memory-mapped image, index it by address minus image base. Never index it with a file offset.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble one function per slot with capstone through the section-data reader and compare mnemonic shapes across the batch. Resolve each direct call against the import table, the verified-rewrite index and earlier lane names. Read each name getter's target as a string and each id getter's immediate, then assert that every slot of one board shares one id. Recover one board's vtable by searching the image for a pointer to a known method and reading the surrounding pointers.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified Halfway through, every name pointer appeared to aim into the middle of unrelated strings, which made the name getter look like anything but a name getter. The cause was my own bug: the memory-mapped image buffer is indexed by address, and I had indexed it with file offsets, silently shifting every data read. Code reads were unaffected because they went through the section-data reader. Re-reading with correct indexing showed every pointer aims exactly at its own board's full name. The wrong readings were discarded and nothing in the final names depends on them.

entry.title: One replay-memory gate verified, and what its proof taught
entry.summary: A per-frame gate in the replay-memory block family passed the full differential proof, and the failures along the way exposed a silent contract trap, a dead computation in the original, and a rule for registers carried across intercepted calls.
entry.content:
A per-frame gate in the replay-memory block family passed the full differential proof, and the failures along the way exposed a silent contract trap, a dead computation in the original, and a rule for registers carried across intercepted calls.

What was asked

Rewrite three neighbouring mid-size functions from the files-memory subsystem in Rust and prove each rewrite identical to the original under the version 4 checker, with a deliberately wrong version run against every proof.

What was found

Verified The smallest of the three, a 369-byte gate with eleven direct calls and one tail jump, passed 1200 of 1200 trials with every check on, and the wrong version failed exactly on the heap as designed.

Verified That gate computes two scaled floats but only ever exposes the first: the range check reads the first product's spill slot while the second product is spilled to a slot nothing reads back. The proof covers every observable behaviour; the dead computation is documented, not hidden.

Verified Global addresses in proof contracts must be written as offsets from the image base, not as full addresses. The full form plants values silently at the wrong place, and every trial then fails the same way a null table would. A five-byte getter and a planted constant confirmed the diagnosis both ways.

Verified A callee that pops fewer words than were pushed is not a mismatch: the extra pushed word was the caller's saved register, which the callee never reads. Its real return cleanup, read from its own epilogue, settled the argument count when push-counting gave the wrong answer.

Inferred The two larger siblings belong to the same family and should verify with the same contract patterns; a complete unprobed contract, rewrite draft, and ordered probe checklist for the middle one is staged for the next lane.

What was decided or recommended

  • Mirror register threading exactly: the original reloads the object register with a selected factor between two poll calls, so the rewrite passes the factor, not the object.
  • Use the stub preserve flag only where the real callee provably preserves the register; skip the comparison with a note where the real body provably ignores it.
  • Pin float operation order from the start and write unordered-aware forms for every float comparison, including threshold tests.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contract generator for the small gate, build the lane crate for the 32-bit target into the lane build folder, and run the driver copy with 1200 trials on the stock worker; then run the bundled wrong version, which must fail on the heap comparison. The staged middle function needs its plan's probe checklist worked first.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first hour looked like the original was at fault: most trials faulted on both sides at once. Two of the causes were mine, a wrong address form and a wrong argument count, and both announced themselves as wild control transfers rather than clean mismatches. The mapping between file offsets and in-memory addresses also bit once at triage time and produced phantom calls until corrected.

entry.title: An aim routine that never returns on a zero offset
entry.summary: One input-ui routine loops forever when its two-dimensional offset is exactly zero, so rewrite proofs must exclude that input by construction; the same lane also learned that a probe passing only on shallow paths proves nothing about deep code.
entry.content:
One input-ui routine loops forever when its two-dimensional offset is exactly zero, so rewrite proofs must exclude that input by construction; the same lane also learned that a probe passing only on shallow paths proves nothing about deep code.

What was asked

Rewrite two neighbouring input-ui functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original over at least one thousand checker trials, with bit-exact float comparison and a deliberately wrong version that must fail.

What was found

Verified The smaller routine, an aim-angle clamp of about six hundred bytes, hangs the original when both components of its computed offset are zero: the magnitude becomes infinite and the angle wrapping loops never terminate. Fixed disjoint value sets for the matrix inputs and the callee outputs keep every trial away from zero, confirmed by a scripted check over all generated trials.

Verified The larger routine, a candidate-pair matcher of about three thousand bytes with fifteen callees, verified on the first attempt. Its proof observes all four computed matrix buffers through call snapshots; ten further words that are verbatim copies of scripted callee answers sit beyond the per-callee snapshot budget and are disclosed as unobserved.

Verified The first rewrite of the smaller routine had two wrapping loops inverted, hanging the rewrite on every trial that reached them, while all twenty-six passing probe trials exited early and never reached the loops. The pass count looked healthy; only the branch-shape count showed the deep code was never exercised.

What was decided or recommended

Both functions verified with the zero-offset input excluded by design and documented, since it hangs the original too. Lanes proving loop-heavy routines should check branch shapes on every probe run, not just the pass count, and should re-derive each loop condition from its exit jump rather than from the entry comparison.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane contract for the aim routine with matrix and callee-output pins drawn from overlapping value sets: trials where the offset comes out as exactly zero hit the trial watchdog on both sides identically. Replace either set with a disjoint one and all trials complete.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two full verification runs sat silent for over forty minutes with no verdict, which first looked like machine overload (more than twenty checker workers were running). A small sixty-trial probe finished quickly and pointed at the inverted loops instead; with the fix, the full run passed in under four minutes. The lesson held twice: small probes diagnose faster than staring at a silent full run.

entry.title: The memory shortage was one forgotten script

entry.content:
For most of a morning the lane count was held down by a shortage of memory that the coordinator put down to the number of lanes and to other programs on the machine. The real cause was one helper script, written by a lane that had finished four hours earlier, still running and holding 8.7 GB. Nine more leftover scripts were each spinning a processor core, some for thirteen hours. Stopping the ten of them took commit headroom from 12 GB to more than 21 and roughly halved processor load.

What was asked

Why only 26 lanes fitted when 45 had fitted the night before on the same machine with similar headroom.

What was found

FactValueWhat it means
Largest leftoverone script, 8.7 GB, four hours oldWritten by a large-function lane to simulate a stack; the lane finished, the script did not
Other leftoversnine scripts, small in memory, each using a full processor coreLoops that never ended; the oldest had run for almost fourteen hours

What was decided or recommended

  • The watchdog now stops any of the project's script processes above 4 GB whatever it is called, and any left by a lane that is no longer running once it is two and a half hours old. It runs on every five-minute tick.
  • A health check runs with every hourly review: leftover and oversized processes, processes that will not exit, memory, commit, page file, disk, the supervisor, the repository. It is now part of the review rule.
  • Only the project's own processes are stopped. Other programs on the machine are reported.

How to reproduce it

List the script and checker processes whose command line points into the project's scratch folders, with their age, memory and processor time; mark each by whether the lane named in its path still has a live agent.

What was confusing or went wrong

The coordinator explained the shortage three times before finding it: first by lane count, then by wrapper processes, then by the owner's other programs, and asked him to close some. Each explanation fitted the totals by process name, because a table grouped by name shows one large group called "python" and nothing says that one member of it is most of the group. The number that should have prompted a closer look was available all along: 26 lanes did not fit where 45 had.

entry.title: Production batch blocked: task-system code span reads encrypted
entry.summary: A production batch of twenty small task-system functions could not be verified because the checker's worker faults on every trial: the code span reads as encrypted bytes through every independent reader, while the project inventory describes valid functions at the same locations.
entry.content:
A production batch of twenty small task-system functions could not be verified because the checker's worker faults on every trial: the code span reads as encrypted bytes through every independent reader, while the project inventory describes valid functions at the same locations.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small neighbouring functions from the task subsystem in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker, deferring with a stated reason where the checker cannot verify.

What was found

Verified The worker faults on the original side of every trial, deterministically, with zero completed original trials, so no verdict could pass. Seventeen rewrites with contracts and one mutant each were completed and banked for re-run; three larger functions were triaged only.

Verified The batch span reads as random-looking bytes through the worker, direct file reads, and repeated hash checks, while other regions of the same file read as normal code and the stock regression passes.

Verified The repaired function inventory matches the banked rewrites exactly on all twenty entries: sizes, instruction counts and callee counts all agree, including shared jump tails and trap jumps. The inventory therefore describes the true code, and the current file bytes in this span do not.

Verified A small set of the lane's own early scripts decoded valid code from this span that matches the inventory exactly, while all other readers saw random bytes from the same path in the same minutes. A long series of controls (identical interpreters, libraries, paths and slices; swapped script contents; fresh nonces proving live execution; stable hashes) failed to find a natural mechanism, and the anomaly is unresolved.

What was decided or recommended

All seventeen completed functions were deferred as needing encrypted code, with rewrites and contracts kept for an unchanged re-run once decrypted bytes are available. Nothing is reported as verified. The coordinator was asked to establish why this span differs from the inventory ground truth, to audit writes to the original file, and to consider having the worker report a hash of its mapped image in every run.

How to reproduce it

Run any of this lane's banked contracts with the stock worker and observe every trial fault on the original side with no completed original trials. Compare the inventory's sizes and instruction counts for the batch against the banked rewrites. Read the lane report in the scratch area for the full control sequence behind the read anomaly.

What was confusing or went wrong

Most of the lane went to the read anomaly: two groups of scripts reading the same file path disagreed about its bytes with perfect script-correlation across dozens of runs, surviving every control that should have distinguished them. The lane stopped investigating at the time box with the mechanism unknown. The practical conclusion does not depend on it: the worker faults, so verification is impossible until the byte mismatch is resolved.
