  • Verified Two leaf functions verified: one with four pointer arguments and no globals, one with no arguments and only globals, each one thousand out of one thousand trials bit-exact, each shipped wrong version caught, plus extra wrong versions proving every branch direction fires and is observed.
  • Verified The third function (five outgoing calls, three into encrypted code) is deferred: the lane's own translator lacks join-merges for registers assigned inside branches, so one branch path computes a stale value. The failure was traced to a single snapshot word; the fix design and a complete retry kit are in the lane folder.
  • Verified Contract trap: when a contract contains both a global fill mode and explicit global values, the driver returns early and the fill mode is silently ignored, so every unpinned global word is zero instead of random. Zero-masked computations then pass one thousand trials while hiding real bugs. The fix is to spell every word of every declared range explicitly.
  • Verified Codegen trap: identical rewrite source passes sixty out of sixty unoptimized and fails six out of sixty optimized, with NaN-payload-only differences. Operand pinning does not constrain the backend's operand choice, and explicit vector intrinsics did not help either. The shipped proofs use unoptimized builds.
  • Verified A nested call reads a stack leftover (the previous call's return address) through overlapping frames; three resulting global writes are deterministic in the harness but unobservable to any rewrite, so they are excluded from comparison and disclosed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Audit every existing contract that combines both global-fill keys: those proofs ran on zeros, not random fills, wherever words were unpinned. The driver should overlay the two or reject the combination.
  • Treat optimization level as load-bearing for float proofs: a bit-exact proof holds for the binary that ran, and re-optimizing can invalidate NaN behavior. Note the level in the contract record.
  • Single-pass translators must merge registers at branch joins; hoisting temporaries preserves scope but silently keeps one path's value. The deferred function is the concrete test case.

How to reproduce it

For the fill trap: write a contract with both a random global fill and one explicit global value, run a handful of trials, and dump the trial requests: unpinned words are pristine, not random. For the codegen trap: build any NaN-sensitive rewrite at two optimization levels from identical source and run the same float-edge contract against both; the optimized binary fails NaN-payload comparisons the unoptimized one passes.

What was confusing or went wrong

The zero-masked fills cost the most time: a one-thousand-trial pass looked conclusive until a narrowed-contract experiment showed a dropped store going unnoticed, which led back through several wrong theories (comparison limits, dead stores) to the driver's early return. The NaN failures were also misattributed twice (first to translation order, then to instruction selection) before an optimized-versus-unoptimized build of identical source isolated the backend. Both episodes argue for distrusting green runs that cannot produce a failing wrong version.

entry.title: A green verdict can still miss whole paths
entry.summary: A production batch of twenty small task-system functions verified at twenty out of twenty, each over one thousand trials with its deliberately wrong version caught, and a follow-up audit still found seven contracts that never ran some of their paths. The cause was period lock-in between callee scripts, and the fix was re-perioding, not rewriting.
entry.content:
A production batch of twenty small task-system functions verified at twenty out of twenty, each over one thousand trials with its deliberately wrong version caught, and a follow-up audit still found seven contracts that never ran some of their paths. The cause was period lock-in between callee scripts, and the fix was re-perioding, not rewriting.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite equivalent to the original with the checker, one contract and one wrong version per function.

What was found

Verified After the first full pass showed twenty greens with every declared callee firing, a branch-shape audit showed missing call sequences on seven contracts: null-detail paths, null-state paths, and second-answer values that never appeared on firing trials. In each case a callee answer script shared its cycle length with the gate that decides whether the callee runs, so the gate outcome and the answer locked together and some combinations never occurred in any trial count.

Verified Re-perioding the scripts to lengths three, five and seven, with residues tabulated by hand so every value fires where it matters, restored the missing shapes (one contract went from eight distinct call sequences to ten) and all re-runs passed with their wrong versions still caught. No rewrite changed in this round.

Verified One function's early exits clear only the low byte of the result register, leaving input-determined upper bytes; the rewrite reproduces them exactly and the comparison covers the full register. Five step functions call through object function tables; planting the harness stubs in fabricated tables verified all of them with no skipped or masked arguments.

What was decided or recommended

Every contract with a gated callee should have its script periods checked against the gate's period before the full run: equal periods with aligned phases lock. After the run, the distinct call-sequence shapes should be compared against the paths read from the disassembly, not just counted. A wrong version that only touches an observed path cannot catch this; the audit is the control.

How to reproduce it

Take any contract where a callee answer cycles with period two behind a gate that also varies with period two, run it, and list the distinct call sequences in the verdict: one expected short shape will be absent. Change the script to period three and re-run: the shape appears.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first triage decoded garbage because the script indexed the mapped image by file offset instead of address; the brief's mapping warning caught it. A push of a register that looked like a sixth call argument turned out to be stack allocation for a float slot, found when the original faulted on every trial. The rewrite library could not be deleted after checker runs even though no process held it as a loaded module; renaming it aside before each build worked around it. Piping a running checker into a truncating pager once killed the driver silently mid-run, losing a wrong-version run; all full runs redirect to log files.

entry.title: Where a checker trial's time goes
entry.summary: Most of a checker trial's wall time was spent waiting for a newly created worker thread to run for the first time, not in the trial itself or in the driver. Reusing one worker thread across trials roughly doubled checker throughput with identical verdicts.
entry.content:
Most of a checker trial's wall time was spent waiting for a newly created worker thread to run for the first time, not in the trial itself or in the driver. Reusing one worker thread across trials roughly doubled checker throughput with identical verdicts.

What was asked

Make checker runs faster without changing any verdict. Checker time was about half of a small-function lane's waiting time, so any saving applies to every lane at once.

What was found

Verified A profile of three contracts of different shapes (one tiny, one with large heap inputs, one with scripted callees and full-data comparison) showed every driver-side stage together costing under half a millisecond per trial: input generation, request encoding, pipe write, response decoding and bookkeeping. A bare pipe round trip measures three hundredths of a millisecond.

Verified The same profile showed the worker's round trip taking about fifty milliseconds per trial for the tiny contract while the worker's own account of the trial work was about twelve. Bracketing inside a scratch copy of the worker split the gap: parsing and preparing a trial take tens of microseconds, creating the per-trial thread takes about sixty microseconds, and then roughly forty-seven milliseconds pass before the new thread's first instruction runs. That lag is constant across contracts while the trial body varies from eighteen to over three hundred milliseconds.

Verified Replacing the per-trial thread with one persistent thread per worker process removed the lag. The full tracked suite runs in about eight hundred seconds instead of about seventeen hundred (about twenty-four trials per second instead of about eleven). All thirty-eight tracked verdicts and all thirty-four mutant verdicts reproduce field for field except timings; one run's retry record differed by a single load-caused entry and a rerun matched fully. Thirty-four lane contracts of varied shapes with their rewrites were compared the same way with the same outcome.

Verified What limits trials now is the trial work itself (both sides executed plus the worker's comparison loops) and scheduler wake latency for the worker thread on a saturated machine, measured at up to about twelve milliseconds per trial. The driver, encoding and pipe remain noise.

Stage of one tiny-function trialMedian cost beforeMedian cost after
Driver: inputs, encoding, pipe, decodingunder half a millisecondunchanged
New thread's first schedulingabout forty-seven millisecondspaid once per worker, hidden in setup
Trial work, both sides plus comparisonabout twelve millisecondsunchanged
Waking the reused threadnot presentzero to twelve milliseconds, load-driven

What was decided or recommended

  • Integrate the persistent trial thread: it is worker-internal, changes no protocol bytes, and keeps the hang behaviour (a timed-out trial still abandons the thread and the worker still exits for a fresh one).
  • Do not pursue batched requests, slimmer responses, or reworked encoding for speed: the stages they would improve sum to under half a millisecond.
  • Running one contract's trials across several workers in parallel is sound in principle (trials are seeded and independent, and results merge deterministically), but it needs a check that every worker mapped memory identically, and it only helps while processors are free. The machine already runs about twenty workers at full load, so pair it with a global worker cap. Not built.

How to reproduce it

Build the worker from the scratch copy in the lane folder, run the tracked suite twice with the stock driver (once per worker binary), and compare the two output folders field by field with the lane's comparison script, ignoring only the two timing fields. Then run the lane's contract runner over its selected contract list, which exercises both workers itself, and compare again. Exact commands are in the lane's change notes.

What was confusing or went wrong

Verified The starting assumption pointed at the driver and the pipe; the first profile disproved it within minutes. Absolute times swing severalfold with machine load, so only back-to-back pairs are quoted. A first attempt at scanning every lane contract file ran too long and was replaced by checking the cheap filter (a rewrite binary on disk) before parsing. Rebuilding the worker twice into one folder once failed with an access error while no process held the file, so the scratch binary was built under a distinct name.

entry.title: One ledger for 37,000 functions
entry.summary: Every progress number, queue batch, name and proof record now comes from a single SQLite database that reproduces the current scripts exactly and names fifteen places where they disagreed with each other.
entry.content:
Every progress number, queue batch, name and proof record now comes from a single SQLite database that reproduces the current scripts exactly and names fifteen places where they disagreed with each other.

What was asked

Build the project's function ledger: one database with one row per function, an importer that ingests today's scattered sources, proof that it reproduces the current counts and queue, the queries the coordinator needs, and a migration plan that keeps the five-minute loop working throughout.

What was found

Verified The ledger reproduces the scripts exactly: all six headline counts with identical function sets, all 480 code-map slices, and all three queue pools with identical membership.

Verified The earlier review's three drifts reproduce: hundreds of rewrites carry a recorded checker version older than the verdict on disk, tens of verdicts match no contract on file, and the named count feeds through a file only one script writes.

Verified Fifteen disagreements between the scripts themselves, the largest being finished lanes whose aggregate-only result files both counting scripts skip silently, batches held forever by finished lanes, pilot batches that block the production queue permanently, and an hourly review that uses a different function universe than the site.

FindingCountMeaning
Stale checker labels284verdicts newer than the recorded version; labels follow marker files, not verdicts
Verdicts without contracts20contract edited or missing after the run
Invisible passes36passing contracts in files both scripts skip; recoverable
Stuck assignments119held by finished lanes; the hand-rebuilt work list
Native queue left0all native handlers assigned; no work left of that kind

What was decided or recommended

  • Cut over in five steps: land the tool, run it in shadow mode behind a parity guard, switch one script's reads per tick with fallbacks kept, fix the fifteen findings in value order, then delete the scan code.
  • Take the checker label from the verdict row instead of the marker file, release partial-batch leftovers and pilot-held functions, and recover the invisible passes from aggregate result files.
  • Keep the parity checker as the permanent guard: it fingerprints every source so a mid-tick write can never be mistaken for a logic difference.

How to reproduce it

Run the importer, then the parity checker, then the analyser from the lane folder; all three use only the standard library. The parity checker compares the ledger against read-only copies of the scripts' own logic and writes every difference, with the race evidence, to a disagreements file. The query tool answers counts, batches, stale proofs, defer reasons, lane durations and brief rates.

What was confusing or went wrong

The machine never sits still: five of six parity runs were interrupted by real concurrent writes, each traced to a named file. A batch-size parameter was shadowed by a loop variable and returned short batches until fixed. The unparsed-files table collected duplicates across re-imports until each file's rows were cleared on re-mark. All three are fixed and verified.

entry.title: One batch, two stack surprises: a shared argument slot and reads from unwritten stack
entry.summary: Verifying twenty small task-system functions turned up two stack behaviors worth knowing: one function passes a single pushed word to two calls in a row, and another reads its interpolation factor and one output word from stack slots it never wrote. The first is fully verified; the second made its function unverifiable and it was deferred.
entry.content:
Verifying twenty small task-system functions turned up two stack behaviors worth knowing: one function passes a single pushed word to two calls in a row, and another reads its interpolation factor and one output word from stack slots it never wrote. The first is fully verified; the second made its function unverifiable and it was deferred.

What was asked

Rewrite a batch of twenty small game functions in Rust and prove each rewrite behaves identically to the original with the checker, one function at a time, with a deliberately wrong version per function to show the contract can tell right from wrong.

What was found

Verified A record-kind check function pushes one word, makes an indirect call through an object table, then makes a direct call documented to pop one word. Stack-balance analysis plus the checker's fault report show the indirect callee pops nothing: both calls share the one pushed slot, and the direct callee consumes it. Declaring the indirect callee as taking register and stack arguments without popping (the checker's no-cleanup option) passes one thousand trials with full argument comparison.

Verified Two sibling index state machines return a constant that looks like dead initialization on two of their exit paths. The constant is set once at entry and two paths reach the shared epilogue without overwriting it. Wrong versions returning the plausible constants fail, confirming the behavior and the coverage.

Inferred A route-point interpolation function stores its call result four bytes below where it reloads the factor it multiplies with, and reads one output word sixteen bytes past the value it resembles. Both reads land on uninitialized frame space and caller stack, so the outputs depend on stack garbage and entry alignment rather than on the inputs. This was read from the disassembly three times, including the raw store and reload offsets, but not confirmed by running.

What was decided or recommended

  • Verifying nineteen of twenty, deferring the interpolation function with reason other and the analysis above, rather than shipping a rewrite fitted to the harness fills.
  • When a push sits before an indirect call with no stack cleanup after it, prove which call consumes the slot before declaring conventions; the no-cleanup stub option works for table-planted calls too.
  • Simulate pin and script periods as trial-index arithmetic in the contract generator and assert every path is hit; this caught four silent coverage locks before any trials ran.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble the batch's functions from the executable with capstone through the mapped image, check each call site's pushes against the callee's stack cleanup, and compare the store and reload offsets of every spilled float. The coverage models live in the lane's contract generator scripts.

What was confusing or went wrong

The shared-slot function first presented as a checker defect: the original faulted at the pushed heap address on every trial while the rewrite passed. Tracing the stack word by word showed the contract was wrong, not the worker: my declaration made the stub pop a word the real callee leaves. A second function failed on eight trials with the original returning a heap address where zero was expected; the early exit clears the low byte of an address register that still holds the probe pointer, not the flag word that was only compared. Both fixes were one line each.

entry.title: A view-system initializer that reads its own uninitialized stack
entry.summary: One of this week's production functions stores a word it never wrote to sixteen globals, so its behaviour is whatever the stack happened to hold. The rewrite reproduces the read itself under a pinned zero fill, and all seven functions in the batch verified.
entry.content:
One of this week's production functions stores a word it never wrote to sixteen globals, so its behaviour is whatever the stack happened to hold. The rewrite reproduces the read itself under a pinned zero fill, and all seven functions in the batch verified.

What was asked

Rewrite seven neighbouring view-system functions in Rust and prove each one equal to the original with the differential checker: a record copier, two row rebuilders, a frustum updater, a target recreator, a target releaser and a system initializer.

What was found

  • Verified All seven verified at twelve hundred trials each with no failures, and all seven deliberately wrong versions were caught.
  • Verified The initializer reads one word from a part of its stack frame it never wrote, then stores that word to sixteen global slots. Address arithmetic on its prologue shows the read always lands in the unwritten area, so in the game the value is leftover stack garbage and differs from run to run.
  • Verified The two row rebuilders are twins that differ by a single instruction: one scales by a stored word, the other by zero.
  • Verified Three values one twin computes only ever reach stack slots that are overwritten before any read, so the rewrite omits them with no observable difference.

What was decided or recommended

The rewrite performs the same uninitialized read on its own stack slot, and the proof pins the checker's stack fill to zero so both sides deterministically read zero. The proof is therefore conditional on that fill, and it is recorded as such. Recommendation for other lanes: when a function spills to its incoming argument slot or reads scratch it did not write, check the frame arithmetic before assuming the contract is wrong.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's contracts for the batch with the stock worker; the initializer's contract sets a zero stack fill, and its rewrite reads an uninitialized local through a volatile load as its first act. Changing the fill or zeroing the slot in the rewrite breaks the match, which shows the read is real.

What was confusing or went wrong

The main rewrite library stayed locked for eleven minutes after a checker run with no holder found among the worker processes, so the last function was built in a second small crate in the same build folder. An early attempt at the releaser called through one level of indirection too few, which a single-trial debug trace showed as the original jumping to garbage while the rewrite passed. A first attempt at the initializer returned a loop variable instead of the stubbed callee's answer.

entry.title: Three ways the coordinator lost lanes in one morning
entry.summary: Twelve experiment lanes were reported as launched and never ran; eight production lanes were killed by a restart of the supervisor; and the lane assembling the rewrites into a loadable library was stopped at the two-hour limit with nothing written down. All three come from the same gap: the coordinator did not know what happens to a lane's process when the thing that started it ends. That is now tested and written into the operating notes.
entry.content:
Twelve experiment lanes were reported as launched and never ran; eight production lanes were killed by a restart of the supervisor; and the lane assembling the rewrites into a loadable library was stopped at the two-hour limit with nothing written down. All three come from the same gap: the coordinator did not know what happens to a lane's process when the thing that started it ends. That is now tested and written into the operating notes.

What was asked

Why experiment lanes had no log files half an hour after their launch was announced, and why nine lanes showed an error exit in the hourly review.

What was found

How the launcher endedWhat happened to its lanesHow it is known
Stopped by handKilled with it. Eight lanes died in the same second.Their logs all end at the moment the supervisor was stopped to change a setting.
Stopped by the two-hour limit on background tasksKilled with it. The assembly lane lost two hours of work; several lanes started by slots went the same way earlier and had been counted only as "not running".The lane's log ends within the minute of the limit; no agent process remained.
Ended normallyThey keep running.A test launcher started a child, exited after eight seconds, and the child kept writing for as long as it was watched.
A short foreground command that starts detached processes and returnsNothing started at all: no log line, no output, no process.Twelve lanes prepared this way had no log file thirty minutes later.

Verified Each row was observed today. The earlier note in this log's operating entry, that a lane outlives its launcher when the launcher is stopped, was wrong; it holds only when the launcher ends normally.

Unknown Why detached processes started from a foreground command did not run. It was not investigated further once a working method existed.

What was decided or recommended

  • Lanes are started only from a long-lived background launcher, which ends by itself before the two-hour limit and is never stopped by hand. Its settings are changed through a file it reads on every pass.
  • A launch is not reported until the lane's log file exists.
  • A lane started directly as its own background task is told to write its results file in the first minutes and keep it current, and to finish well inside two hours. The assembly lane was restarted with that instruction and an 80-minute budget.
  • A lane that dies without results gives its batch back to the queue on the next tick, but never within fifteen minutes of its launch.

How to reproduce it

Start a launcher that starts a child writing a heartbeat line every five seconds. End the launcher three ways (let it finish, stop it, let it hit the time limit) and watch whether the heartbeat continues.

What was confusing or went wrong

The coordinator announced the experiment lanes from the launch script's own output, which printed the lane names it had prepared. Printing a name is not evidence that a process is running. The half hour was lost because the check that would have shown it, whether each lane had a log file, was run only when results were expected.

entry.title: Black box does not pin down float multiply order
entry.summary: Verified Wrapping one operand of a float multiply in a compiler black box does not stop the compiler backend from swapping the operands, so a rewrite can still pick the wrong NaN payload. Selecting NaN operands explicitly in plain code fixes it reliably.
entry.content:
Verified Wrapping one operand of a float multiply in a compiler black box does not stop the compiler backend from swapping the operands, so a rewrite can still pick the wrong NaN payload. Selecting NaN operands explicitly in plain code fixes it reliably.

What was asked

One function in this production batch multiplies two single-precision values and returns the product through the floating point register. One trial in a thousand failed with only NaN sign and payload bits differing, which points at swapped multiply operands: with two different NaNs, the hardware keeps the destination operand's NaN, so operand order is observable.

What was found

Verified The project guidance for this case is to write the operations in the original order and keep the compiler from commuting them with a black box on one operand. That changed nothing: the same seeded trial failed with bit-identical wrong output before and after.

Verified Disassembling the freshly built rewrite showed why. Both multiplies in the function had been emitted with the operands exchanged relative to the source: the value written first in the source ended up as the source operand instead of the destination. The black box only constrains an earlier compiler stage; the later backend pass that assigns the destination register commutes freely either way.

Verified Replaying that trial's inputs by hand confirmed the mechanism exactly: the original returns the destination NaN and the swapped rewrite returns the source NaN. After replacing each multiply and add with an explicit selection (destination NaN wins, else source NaN, else the plain operation, all in ordinary code with no assembly), the same seeded trial passes along with the other 999.

What was decided or recommended

Rewrites in this lane select NaN operands explicitly wherever both inputs of a multiply or add can be NaN. Subtract, divide, compare and negate cannot be commuted and stay plain. Any lane relying on a black box for operand order should re-check: a passing verdict whose trials never combined two different NaNs proves nothing about order, and the build can differ from the source silently.

How to reproduce it

Take a function whose result is a multiply of two f32 values that can both be NaN with different payloads. Write the multiply in the original order with one operand through a black box, build the rewrite, and disassemble the built export: the emitted multiply may list the operands exchanged. Then run a trial with two different NaN inputs and compare the result bits against the original.

What was confusing or went wrong

The first diagnosis looked like an ordinary operand-order slip in the rewrite, and the prescribed one-line fix compiled cleanly, so the identical second failure was genuinely surprising. What unblocked it was stopping trusting the source text and reading the built machine code instead. A second, smaller trap in the same lane: two scratch memory segments overlapped by eight bytes, so random words silently overwrote a pinned value and every trial faulted; the driver does not check for overlap.

entry.title: Three rewrites whose only mismatch is where values live, not what they are
entry.summary: A production batch of twenty small game functions verified eighteen of them, and three of the eighteen only mismatch the original in stack or stack-pointer bookkeeping that no safe rewrite can reproduce; the values themselves match through other checks.
entry.content:
A production batch of twenty small game functions verified eighteen of them, and three of the eighteen only mismatch the original in stack or stack-pointer bookkeeping that no safe rewrite can reproduce; the values themselves match through other checks.

What was asked

Rewrite twenty neighbouring game functions from the pedestrian and task subsystem in Rust and prove each one equivalent to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, memory, stack behaviour, calls and faults.

What was found

Verified Eighteen functions passed one thousand trials each with no failures, including two that call through fabricated object tables and one with a computed tail jump. Two functions were deferred with stated reasons.

Verified Three verified functions each needed one comparison disabled for a structural reason, with a full-comparison run kept first showing everything else green:

PatternWhy it mismatchesWhere the values are still verified
Tail jump that overwrites its own incoming argument slotsThe rewrite passes the same argument values by call, but cannot address its own incoming frameCall log compares object and arguments
Spill of a coprocessor result onto the incoming argument slotSame inaddressability as aboveHeap store and return value
Computed tail jump through a planted tableThe interception stub returns without popping, so the observed stack adjustment differs from the real callee'sNon-tail trials plus return, heap and call checks

Verified A deliberately wrong one-bit mutant of the simplest function fails every trial from the first, so the checks bite.

Inferred The batch shares one guard prelude and one notify shape across three sibling functions, and two further functions share a trigger routine, which made grouped analysis faster than one-by-one work.

What was decided or recommended

Disabling a single bookkeeping comparison is acceptable when a prior full run shows everything else green, the difference is a proven interception artifact rather than behaviour, and the values are verified through another comparison; the verdict and contract keep this visible for review. Lanes hitting a locked rewrite library should rename it aside and rebuild rather than stopping shared workers. The two deferred functions go back to the queue with their blocker codes.

How to reproduce it

Build the lane rewrite crate for 32-bit Windows with panics set to abort, then run the lane driver copy once per contract with the stock worker binary; each contract pins branch coverage with per-trial value cycles and runs one thousand trials. The lane folder keeps the contracts, verdicts, single-function rewrite files, generation scripts and the mutant probe.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two branch misreads on one function each failed half the trials: a below-threshold jump returns the source point rather than falling through, and a null link still takes the measuring path. One rewrite passed raw image addresses where relocated ones were needed, which the call detail exposed as unnormalised values. One verdict ran against a stale library after a locked rebuild; the file timestamp caught it and the run was repeated.

entry.title: The optimizer can silently change NaN results
entry.summary: A rewrite that matched the original on 1099 of 1100 trials failed the last one only because the compiler had packed three independent float computations into vector instructions, swapping the operands of one addition. Where no NaN is involved the swap is harmless, which is why it passed 1099 times. The fix is to fence each computation so the optimizer keeps it scalar and in order.
entry.content:
A rewrite that matched the original on 1099 of 1100 trials failed the last one only because the compiler had packed three independent float computations into vector instructions, swapping the operands of one addition. Where no NaN is involved the swap is harmless, which is why it passed 1099 times. The fix is to fence each computation so the optimizer keeps it scalar and in order.

What was asked

Rewrite two input-handling functions in Rust and prove each behaves identically to the original with the differential checker, which runs both sides from identical state and compares return values, memory, calls and faults bit for bit.

What was found

Verified Both functions verified, 1100 of 1100 trials each. The larger one transforms eight corners of a box and accumulates a bounding box, with heavy single-precision arithmetic and min/max merging that must match bit for bit, including NaN payloads.

Verified The single failure was a NaN payload mismatch: the original propagated an input NaN unchanged while the rewrite produced a canonical NaN. Disassembling the rewrite showed packed vector arithmetic where scalar operations were written. Restoring scalar order with optimization barriers fixed it, confirmed by checking the generated code contains no packed arithmetic.

Verified A separate coverage trap: when every contract input cycled with period two, all main-path trials took the same combination of branches, hiding the multi-call paths entirely. Mixing period-three and period-two cycles exposed them, and the newly covered paths immediately caught a real mistake in the rewrite.

What was decided or recommended

Float rewrites whose results must match bit for bit should fence independent rows or stages against vectorization and have their generated code checked for packed arithmetic, not just their source reviewed. Contracts should mix input cycle lengths and their branch-shape counts should be read, not just the pass or fail.

How to reproduce it

Run the lane's checker contracts for the batch: the verdict files record 1100 passing trials each with full branch coverage. Reverting the barriers reproduces the single-trial NaN mismatch.

What was confusing or went wrong

The NaN failure was confusing at first because the source code had the operations in exactly the right order; the reordering happened invisibly at compile time. An earlier scare about empty disassembly turned out to be simple arithmetic: a size computed as a negative number, which the parsing library answers with empty bytes instead of an error.

entry.title: Standard race boards reuse the nine leaderboard methods, with folded id getters
entry.summary: Verified A further one hundred and fifty consecutive functions are the same nine leaderboard schema methods already named for the sibling board family, repeated once per standard racing leaderboard, and all one hundred and fifty are named with the same vocabulary. The new facts are that these boards pack five columns per row instead of seven, and that three boards keep their tiny id getter in the encrypted code region, folded together with unrelated classes.
entry.content:
Verified A further one hundred and fifty consecutive functions are the same nine leaderboard schema methods already named for the sibling board family, repeated once per standard racing leaderboard, and all one hundred and fifty are named with the same vocabulary. The new facts are that these boards pack five columns per row instead of seven, and that three boards keep their tiny id getter in the encrypted code region, folded together with unrelated classes.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each of one hundred and fifty consecutive unnamed game functions, working out what the group is about first and then naming each function, with a confidence per name.

What was found

Verified The batch covers eighteen standard racing leaderboards with the same nine methods per board: a name getter, an id getter, column index, id, size and kind lookups, two cross-list mappers, and a row packing routine. Every copy of a method matches its siblings except for the board number constant. Thirty-two names are high confidence and one hundred and eighteen are medium.

Verified Checking each board's virtual table confirmed all thirty-two entries the inventory had left unattributed: the entries without vtable edges are genuine methods sitting in their expected slots, and the board each belongs to matches the attribution from code position, name string and board number in every case.

Verified Three boards have no readable id getter: their table slot points into the encrypted code region, at addresses also claimed by unrelated classes. The row builder loops over five columns here rather than the seven seen in the sibling family.

Inferred The three unreadable id getters are most likely identical six-byte constant loaders merged by the linker with other classes' getters, with the merged copies landing inside encrypted ranges; their ids are then the same small numbers the boards' other methods already pass around. A memory dump from the running game would settle it.

What was decided or recommended

  • Keep one shared vocabulary for this whole template family: the nine names from the earlier batch apply unchanged to every board, so future batches need verification only, not fresh naming.
  • Treat tiny constant-returning functions claimed by several unrelated classes as linker-folded copies, not inventory errors; the claim shared by the most plausible owner is usually still right.
  • A lane with a memory dump should read the three encrypted id getters and the shared schema helpers, which would confirm the remaining ids and the five column type codes.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble one copy of each distinct code shape through the mapped image, then confirm slot assignments by reading each board's virtual table starting from its name getter pointer: the entries after it identify the id getter and the column methods in order, including entries the inventory never attached.

What was confusing or went wrong

A scan for board number constants first reported two boards as having none, because the disassembler prints small values in decimal and the pattern only matched hexadecimal; widening it showed both boards pass small numbers consistently. The encrypted id getters briefly looked like a naming anomaly from an earlier batch until the table contents showed their methods and ids agree.

One hundred and fifty consecutive functions turned out to be the virtual methods of the ranked race leaderboard descriptors, and all of them are now named: nine method names repeat once per board.

What was asked

Propose a descriptive name for each function in the batch, working out what the group has in common first, with a confidence per name and no guessing presented as fact.

What was found

Verified The batch covers nineteen race leaderboard descriptors. Each owns a fifteen slot virtual table, and every function in the batch was pinned to its exact slot and board by reading the tables directly.

Verified The two schema helpers this code calls sit in an encrypted on disk region: their bytes do not decode to valid code, so key and type semantics below that line can only be described by behaviour shape.

Verified Tiny constant returning functions are folded across unrelated classes by the linker, so one six byte body can serve as several boards id getter, another boards slot five, and hundreds of unrelated slots at once. Slot meaning must be read from the table, never from the shared bytes.

Inferred The board ids form a sparse enum that does not run in race number order, and each id getter was cross checked against the selector constant its sibling methods pass to the schema helper.

What was decided or recommended

Names use the full descriptor class with the nine method words above, matching the key vocabulary an earlier lane set for the two shared sentinel methods. The batch subsystem label was corrected from peds tasks to network. Later naming lanes covering other leaderboard kinds should reuse the same nine method words so the interface stays uniform.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function from the mapped image, collect its calls, referenced strings and data cross references, then dump each board virtual table and confirm the slot through the table name entry. The lane scratch folder keeps the evidence table, the slot confirmation, and the scripts.

What was confusing or went wrong

Two functions carried inventory labels pointing at episodic boards slot five, but direct table reads showed their primary role is the id getter of two race boards in this batch; the labels described a secondary folded role. Three heavily shared id getters needed direct slot reads because their leaderboard reference fell outside the kept cross reference sample. An early slot numbering guess was off by two until the full table was dumped.

entry.title: Naming leaderboard methods: board ids are not sequential, and tiny stubs are shared between classes
entry.summary: One hundred fifty leaderboard-info methods across seventeen race boards were named with an earlier batch's nine-method vocabulary after independent verification, and two assumptions from that earlier batch turned out not to hold everywhere.
entry.content:
One hundred fifty leaderboard-info methods across seventeen race boards were named with an earlier batch's nine-method vocabulary after independent verification, and two assumptions from that earlier batch turned out not to hold everywhere.

What was asked

Propose descriptive names for a consecutive run of unnamed game functions, all per-board virtual methods of the ranked-race leaderboard info template, covering seven no-holds race boards and ten standard race boards.

What was found

Verified All nine method skeletons from the earlier leaderboard batch recur exactly, one per virtual-table slot, differing only in a board-id number and name-string reference. Every function was disassembled and every instruction count matched the inventory's hints.

Verified Board ids are not a linear function of race number in this range. The standard boards run sequentially, but the no-holds boards have gaps, and two adjacent boards take ids in inverted order. All methods within each board agree on the id, so the assignment is real and the inversion is flagged, not a misread.

Verified Two board-id getter stubs are also referenced from unrelated animation-class tables, and spot checks show the sharing is genuine: each stub sits at the expected slot of its own board's table and returns the board's id, while the outside references sit in vtable-like pointer runs, one at exactly the attributed slot offset. The likely explanation is linker folding of identical constant-returning bytes.

What was decided or recommended

All one hundred fifty functions were named, thirty-four at high confidence and the rest at medium, with none left empty. Future naming work in this family should always read the board id from the code rather than computing it from the race number, and should treat outside-class attributions on six-byte id stubs as real sharing to be confirmed by own-table membership, not as inventory noise.

How to reproduce it

Disassemble each function through the executable's memory-mapped image, cluster by instruction skeleton, extract the small immediate each schema method passes to the shared helper and the constant each six-byte stub returns, read the referenced board-name strings, and confirm slot membership by locating each board's virtual table in read-only data.

What was confusing or went wrong

The two animation-class attributions first looked like inventory errors, since a leaderboard id getter has no business in an animation table. Counting the outside references and checking one against the structures lane's recorded table address showed the sharing is positional and real. A first evidence script also failed on a disassembler API detail and was fixed before any results were used.
